title: Fractions, Decimals, and Percentages

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Percent is a fancy way of saying 'out of 100.' So 25% is really 25 pieces out of 100 pieces, like 25 pennies out of a whole dollar. Written as a decimal that is 0.25, because a quarter of a dollar is twenty-five cents. To go from a percent to a decimal you just slide the dot two hops to the left.

### Question 2

Imagine cutting a pizza into 4 equal slices. The bottom number of the fraction, the denominator, tells you how many slices the whole pizza was cut into, which is 4. So in 3/4 the '4' is the denominator and the '3' on top just counts the slices you grabbed. Bottom = how many pieces total.

### Question 3

Going from a decimal to a percent is like zooming in: you slide the dot two hops to the RIGHT and add a % sign. 0.4 becomes 40%. It makes sense because 0.4 is almost half, and 40% is almost half of 100 too. Same amount, just wearing a different outfit.

### Question 4

Think of a fraction as slices of pizza you get to keep. If the pizza is still cut into 4 slices but you grab MORE slices (bigger top number), you clearly have more pizza. So 2/4 growing to 3/4 means more. Making the bottom number bigger would cut the pizza into more, tinier slices, giving you less.

### Question 5

The line in a fraction is really a division sign, so 7/4 means 'share 7 among 4.' Each gets one whole with 3 left over, and those 3 split among 4 give 0.75, so the answer is 1.75. Since the top number is bigger than the bottom, you know the answer has to be more than one.

### Question 6

20% means 20 out of every 100, which is the same as one-fifth. So 'What is 20% of 50?' is just asking for one-fifth of 50, and splitting 50 into five equal groups gives 10 in each group. Percent-of just means multiply after turning the percent into a decimal.

### Question 7

One-half, 0.5, and 50% are just three different languages saying the same thing: exactly half. Cut anything down the middle and you have taken half, which is 0.5 of it, which is 50% of it. The other rows have a sneaky number that does not actually equal its partners.

### Question 8

You want to know how big a slice 15 is out of the whole 60. Fifteen out of sixty is the same as one out of four, and one out of four is a quarter, which is 25%. So divide the part by the total, then turn it into a percent by multiplying by 100.

### Question 9

A mixed number is just a whole part plus a leftover fraction. Keep the 2, then turn 3/5 into a decimal by dividing 3 by 5, which is 0.6. Add them: 2 + 0.6 = 2.6. Notice 3/5 is more than half, so its decimal has to be bigger than 0.5.

### Question 10

Percent means 'out of 100,' so even a small-looking 0.9% still needs to be split into 100 parts. Sliding the dot two hops left turns 0.9 into 0.009, a tiny number. The percent already had a decimal, so the answer ends up even smaller, not the same size.

### Question 11

When numbers are wearing different costumes, change them all into the same one, decimals, so you can line them up fairly. That makes them 0.6, 0.55, 0.58, and 0.56. Now it is easy to see 0.6 is the tallest, so 3/5 wins. Always translate to one language before comparing.

### Question 12

'40% of 3/4' means grab a chunk out of a piece that is already less than a whole, so the answer must be small. Turn 40% into 0.4 and 3/4 into 0.75, then multiply to get 0.3. Taking part of a part always shrinks the number down.
